cases.abstract: Visual imitation policies trained on few demonstrations lack corrective supervision when execution drifts from expert trajectories. DMD extends that supervision by synthesizing nearby wrist-camera views and assigning actions toward later expert poses. A pretrained diffusion model is adapted on task data, exploratory play, or both; reconstructed camera geometry links each requested viewpoint change to its action label. Using a later target reduces backward-pointing labels when a generated pose has overshot the next frame. Hardware tests span pushing, stacking, pouring, shirt hanging, and cup arrangement. For apple pushing, DMD succeeds in all ten trials versus three for behavior cloning. With eight task demonstrations and a generator adapted only on play data, success is 80% versus 20%. For five unseen cups in a new laboratory, augmenting Diffusion Policy increases success from 4/25 to 16/25 under matched rectified, center-cropped inputs. These comparisons support adding corrective supervision around recoverable deviations, including under object and environment shift. The recoverability condition matters: returning to an expert pose cannot undo irreversible failures such as spilling.
cases.methods: DMD augments the states a policy sees without requiring new expert actions at each state: it combines pose-conditioned view synthesis with geometric relabeling. Structure from motion recovers camera poses from demonstrations, yielding image pairs and relative transforms for adapting a pretrained diffusion model; the latent-image codebook stays fixed. A sampled displacement then defines a virtual wrist-camera pose near an observed frame. Rather than merely reversing that displacement, the label maps the virtual pose to a later pose on the expert trajectory, coupling correction with continued task progress. The later target matters when synthesis moves past the next demonstrated pose: labeling toward that pose could command backward motion. The pushing ablation favors a three-frame lookahead, after which error plateaus. Original and synthesized image-action pairs are combined for policy training, extending supervision to nearby deviations assumed to remain recoverable.
cases.results: Pouring tests whether synthesized supervision improves coordination during rotation, rather than merely reproducing successful approach motions. After adapting the view generator on 49 demonstrations and 16 play trajectories, DMD transfers all 57 grams of beans in 80% of trials, compared with 0% for behavior cloning in their randomized pairwise test. The baseline often rotates the source cup without moving it toward the receiver, letting positional errors accumulate; DMD's higher completion rate is consistent with better correction during this phase. A separate test using a generator adapted only on task data yields 70% success for DMD versus 30% for behavior cloning. Augmentation therefore improves completion in both tested data regimes, while the differing baseline rates prevent reading DMD's 80% and 70% as a controlled estimate of the benefit of play data. The recoverability assumption remains consequential: directing the robot back toward an expert pose cannot restore beans spilled before correction.
cases.notes: Retained the recovery-supervision argument rather than making view quality the contribution. Pose-label rationale: Sections III-C and IV-A3b, Figures 5 and 8. Table II: pushing uses ten trials per method, with play-only generator adaptation at eight demonstrations. Table V: 25 trials on five unseen cups; both policies use rectified center crops. Table IV: pouring comparisons are separate randomized A/B tests, so baseline changes block a controlled play-data comparison. Labels assume recoverability and cannot reverse spilling. Replaced the initial Results reference to image prediction error: the offline metric is action-direction error.

cases.abstract: Fine bimanual manipulation requires demonstrations and learned policies that preserve precision over long, high-frequency trajectories. ALOHA supplies open-source teleoperation within a $20,000 budget, mapping smaller leader arms directly to follower joint positions to avoid reliance on inverse kinematics near singularities. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) learns sequences of joint targets from these demonstrations, shortening the effective decision horizon. It combines overlapping predictions for the same timestep to incorporate visual feedback without abrupt chunk switches, and uses conditional variational training to accommodate human trajectory variation. Evaluation covers two simulated tasks and six hardware tasks, with 50 demonstrations per hardware task except 100 for Thread Velcro. In 25-trial hardware tests, ACT achieves 88% success opening a sliding ziploc bag and 96% inserting a battery; four comparison methods never progress beyond the first stage. A six-participant study finds shorter completion times with 50Hz than 5Hz leader updates. Yet ACT succeeds on only 20% of Thread Velcro trials, and initial candy-unwrapping tests produce no complete successes in ten attempts. The system extends learned fine manipulation to several tested tasks while retaining substantial perception and force limitations.
cases.methods: ACT predicts a fixed-length sequence of absolute joint targets from four camera views and current follower joint positions, reducing the effective prediction horizon. The training targets come from the leader arms: leader-follower discrepancies drive force through the motor controllers, so recording follower motion would discard part of the commanded interaction. A conditional variational encoder represents demonstration variability through a latent style variable, while the transformer policy reconstructs the chunk under Gaussian-prior regularization. At deployment, the encoder is discarded and the latent variable is fixed at zero. To avoid waiting for an entire chunk before updating observations, ACT is queried every timestep, and overlapping predictions for the current execution time are exponentially weighted and averaged. This incorporates observations continuously while moderating abrupt chunk transitions. Combining predictions of the same target, rather than actions at neighboring times, also avoids blending distinct stages of the intended motion.
cases.results: ACT's ablations distinguish gains from sequence prediction from gains tied to learning variable human behavior. With temporal ensembling disabled, success averaged over two simulated tasks and both scripted and human datasets rises from 1% with single-step prediction to 44% with 100-step chunks. Larger chunks slightly reduce success, consistent with a tradeoff between shortening the horizon and retaining reactive control. BC-ConvMLP and VINN also improve with chunking, so its benefit is not confined to ACT's transformer architecture. In a separate comparison on the two simulated tasks, removing conditional variational training reduces success with human data from 35.3% to 2%, while scarcely changing results with scripted data. That contrast supports using the objective for human demonstrations, not assuming equal benefits for deterministic data. After separate hyperparameter tuning, temporal ensembling adds 3.3 percentage points to ACT's best average success and four to BC-ConvMLP's, but hurts VINN. Thus the evidence favors shorter effective horizons and variability-aware training in these settings, while rejecting uniformly beneficial prediction averaging or ever-longer chunks.
cases.notes: Retained hardware access and policy learning; explained direct joint mapping rather than listing components. Tables II-III: hardware comparisons use one seed and 25 trials; simulation uses three seeds with 50 evaluations each. Figure 9: chunking excludes temporal ensembling, ensemble configurations are separately tuned, and CVAE gains differ by demonstration source. Thread Velcro uses 100 demonstrations. Candy unwrapping's initial 0/10 differs from 3/5 candies opened with ten attempts per candy. The 5Hz study samples leaders at 5Hz but sends interpolated targets at 50Hz. Reconstruction-loss reporting differs between implementation (L1) and pseudocode (MSE); no loss choice is asserted.
